en: The Sūtra on Departing from Sleep, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at the Mṛgadāva (Deer Park) in Vārāṇasī.
In a forest grove.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was in the village of Sāṅkassa in Magadha.

While the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was walking back and forth alone in a quiet place, he fell asleep; the Blessed One knew that the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was walking back and forth alone in a quiet place and had fallen asleep.

At that time, the Blessed One, knowing that the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was alone in a quiet place, walking to and fro, and had fallen asleep, immediately entered a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) corresponding to his form. With a mind in *samādhi*, just as a strong man might bend or extend his arm, the Blessed One likewise vanished from the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in Vārāṇasī and suddenly appeared before the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana in the village of Sāṅkassa in Magadha.
At that time, the Blessed One arose from samādhi and addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"Maudgalyāyana! Maudgalyāyana!"
“Do you wish to sleep? “Indeed,
World-Honored One.”
"Why do you wish to sleep because of such thoughts?
Do not engage in conceptualization, do not engage in discursive thought, and do not engage in excessive proliferation; in this way, sleep shall be abandoned."

If you cannot free yourself from sleep, then you, Moggallāna, should extensively recite and practice the Dharma as you have heard it and as you have memorized it; in this way, you shall be freed from sleep.
"If you cannot abandon it, then you, Moggallāna, should extensively explain to others the Dharma as you have heard it and the Dharma as you have recited it; in this way, sleep shall be abandoned."
"If you cannot free yourself from it, then you, Moggallāna, should reflect upon and practice the Dharma as you have recited it and as you have heard it; in this way, sleep shall be abandoned."
If it does not leave you, Moggallāna, you should wash your eyes and your limbs with cold water; thus, sleep shall depart.
If it still does not leave you, Moggallāna!
"You should pull both ears with both hands; thus, sleep shall depart.
If it does not depart, you, Moggallāna, should rise and go out from the lecture hall, look toward the four quarters, and observe the stars; thus, sleep shall depart."

If you cannot free yourself from it, then you, Moggallāna, should wander about in an open space, guard your sense faculties, and direct your mind toward acts of giving; later, by forming such a perception, you shall be free from sleep.
"If you cannot leave it, then you, Moggallāna, should go back and wander about in solitude;
having folded up your sitting mat (niṣīdana) and spread it upon the bed, sit cross-legged, and thus sleep so as to leave it."
"If you cannot leave, then you, Maudgalyāyana, should return to the lecture hall,

fold your *uttarāsaṅga* robe in four layers and spread it upon the bed, place your *saṃghāṭī* robe at the head of the bed, lie on your right side with one foot resting upon the other, maintain the perception of light, keep your mind undistracted, and remain mindful with the thought of rising."
“Moggallāna! Do not delight in beds;
do not delight in sleeping on your right side; do not delight in sleep; do not delight in taking worldly honor as a flavor.”
For what reason? Maudgalyāyana!
I do not say that one should approach all dharmas, nor do I say that one should not approach all dharmas.
"How is it, Maudgalyāyana!
Do I not say that one does not draw near to any phenomena?
You, Maudgalyāyana!"
I say that one should not associate with laypeople.

Maudgalyāyana! If one dwells associating with laypeople, there will be only the sharing of discourses but no sharing of recitation; because of those discourses, there arises flattery and arrogance; because of arrogance, there arises envy; and because of envy, one does not know how to rest.
"O Maudgalyāyana! If one does not bring [the mind] to rest, one becomes distant from samādhi.
Maudgalyāyana, this is what I call a dharma that should not be cultivated."
"What do you think, Maudgalyāyana!
What is it that I call the practice of associating with [wholesome] dharmas? Maudgalyāyana!"
"When you have reached a place of profound stillness, make a bed of grass and remain silent, free from all evils and separated from the crowds; you should always sit in contemplation.
This, Maudgalyāyana, is what it means."
I speak of the practice of association. "Maudgalyāyana!
When entering a village for alms, you should not seek profit or reward, nor should you seek honor."
"O Maudgalyāyana! Having satisfied your mind with the merit of this respectful offering, you should now enter the village to beg for alms. O Maudgalyāyana!"
When entering a village for alms, you must not enter another's house with conceptual thoughts.
Why is this, Maudgalyāyana?
A householder’s home has many worldly affairs.
If a bhikṣu enters a householder’s home and they do not speak with him, that bhikṣu then thinks:
"Who has told this householder against me, such that he does not speak with me?"
"Then there arises a mind of anger; once there is anger, there is arrogance; because of arrogance, there is lack of tranquility. Maudgalyāyana!
When the mind lacks tranquility, one becomes distant from samādhi."
"O Maudgalyāyana! When you preach the Dharma, you should not perceive victory or defeat; you should maintain a mind of non-victory.
If you harbor a mind of victory, there will be much disputation; from much disputation comes arrogance; from arrogance comes envy; and from envy comes lack of tranquility."
"Maugandalyāyana!
When there is no longer cessation, I speak of the samādhi of seclusion.
You, Maugandalyāyana!"
When preaching the Dharma, one should speak for the benefit of others, one should speak with certainty, one should not speak as others do, and one should discourse like the lion’s roar.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!
"You should train yourselves thus.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, adjusted his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"O Blessed One!"
“How does a bhikkhu reach the ultimate end, reach ultimate purity, and practice the holy life to its ultimate conclusion?

“Moggallāna, if a bhikkhu experiences any bodily sensation—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he should contemplate that sensation as impermanent; he should contemplate it as subject to decay; he should contemplate it as unsoiled; he should contemplate it as subject to cessation; he should contemplate it as right; he should contemplate it as the place of stilling. In this way, he should contemplate that sensation.”

One should contemplate that this feeling is not permanent; one should contemplate it as subject to decay; one should contemplate it as undefiled; one should contemplate it as exhaustion; one should contemplate it as cessation; one should contemplate it as subsiding. Thus, one does not cling to this world; not clinging, one is not afraid;

being without fear, one attains parinirvāṇa through the relinquishing of the remainder of existence. Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and name-and-form are known according to reality.
"This is it, monk Maudgalyāyana!
This is the ultimate end, the ultimate stainlessness, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate practice of the holy life.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Blessed One had spoken, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana rejoiced and was delighted.
*The Discourse on Freedom from Drowsiness* Spoken by the Buddha.
